title: Authentication & Authorization
description: Understand sessions, tokens, JWT structure, OAuth 2.0 flows, OpenID Connect, and refresh token strategies.

segments.text: Authentication asks 'who are you?' Authorization asks 'what can you do?' These two questions underpin every secure system. Let's explore how the web answers them.

The classic approach is session-based auth. You log in, the server creates a session, stores it in memory, and gives you a session ID in a cookie. Every subsequent request sends that cookie automatically.

Sessions work great for a single server. But with multiple servers behind a load balancer, which server has your session? You need sticky sessions or a shared session store like Redis. It gets complicated fast.

Token-based auth flips the model. Instead of the server remembering you, it gives you a signed token containing your identity. The server is stateless — it just verifies the token's signature on each request.

JWT — JSON Web Token — is the standard. It has three parts separated by dots. The header specifies the algorithm. The payload carries claims like user ID and expiration. The signature prevents tampering. It's all base64-encoded.
Important catch — JWTs are signed, not encrypted. Anyone can read the payload. Never put sensitive data like passwords in a JWT. The signature only proves nobody tampered with it.
segments.thought_prompt: If JWTs are stateless, how would you revoke a token before it expires?

segments.text: OAuth 2.0 solves a different problem — delegated access. 'Let this app read my Google calendar without giving it my Google password.' OAuth lets users grant limited access to their resources on one service to another service.

The authorization code flow is the most secure. The user is redirected to the auth server, logs in, gets a code. Your backend exchanges that code for tokens. The user's credentials never touch your application.

OpenID Connect builds on top of OAuth. While OAuth only handles authorization, OIDC adds an identity layer. It returns an ID token that tells your app who the user is — their name, email, profile picture.

Access tokens expire quickly — minutes to hours. Refresh tokens last longer and let you get new access tokens without re-authenticating. Store them securely. If a refresh token leaks, an attacker has persistent access.
Rotating refresh tokens add another layer. Each time you use a refresh token, you get a new one and the old one is invalidated. If someone steals and uses the old one, the system detects the breach.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is refresh token rotation better than just having a long-lived access token?

segments.text: Sessions for simplicity, JWTs for statelessness, OAuth for delegation, OIDC for identity. Each solves a different piece of the puzzle. Understanding when to use which is what separates a good engineer from a great one.
